candidates.candidate_text: Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals into Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigeria Customs Service.
Transportation of cash or negotiable instruments in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent by individuals out of Nigeria shall be declared to the Nigeria Customs Service.

False declaration or failure to make the required declaration to the Nigeria Customs Service is an offence that may lead on conviction to forfeiture of the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument, imprisonment for at least two years, or both.
candidates.reviewed_text: Any person who falsely declares or fails to make a declaration to the Nigeria Customs Service under section 12 of the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act commits an offence and is liable on conviction to forfeit the undeclared funds or negotiable instrument or to imprisonment for a term of at least two years or both.

candidates.candidate_text: The reviewed official CBN guidance states that the declaration rule for cash or negotiable instruments above US$10,000 does not itself prohibit genuinely owned or obtained funds above that amount from being brought into Nigeria or taken outside the country.

Where foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 is imported in cash and deposited into a domiciliary account with an authorised dealer, the account may only be withdrawn from in cash and that imported cash is exportable from Nigeria only in cash.
candidates.reviewed_text: Where a person imports foreign currency in excess of US$10,000 or its equivalent in cash and not by means of a bank draft, mail or telegraphic transfer and deposits the foreign currency in a domiciliary account with an authorised dealer, withdrawals from that account may be made only in cash, and that imported cash is exportable from Nigeria only in cash.

candidates.candidate_text: The importation and exportation of the naira remain prohibited except as permitted under guidelines issued from time to time by the Central Bank.

human_review.notes: M2.5 supported as s.14 baseline only; numeric exception remains not established.

candidates.candidate_text: Current Customs operational guidance uses a declaration trigger of US$10,000 or more, which conflicts with the statutory phrase in excess of US$10,000.
candidates.reviewed_text: Current Customs operational guidance on the e-currency declaration form uses a declaration trigger of US$10,000 or more / equal to or greater than US$10,000.

human_review.notes: M2.5 bounded to Customs operational >= trigger; dual-operator preservation remains an I-B source-layer disposition.

candidates.candidate_text: The earlier Foreign Exchange Act wording requiring declaration only when foreign currency exceeds US$5,000 is a legacy threshold retained for temporal audit and should not be used as the current border-cash rule while MLPPA 2022 is operative.
candidates.reviewed_text: FEMMPA 1995 section 12 states that foreign currency in excess of US$5,000 or its equivalent, whether being imported into or exported out of Nigeria, shall be declared on the prescribed form for reasons of statistics only. That older threshold wording is retained for temporal audit and must not drive the current border-cash declaration threshold while MLPPA 2022 section 3(3) uses in excess of US$10,000.

candidates.candidate_text: Any person may open, maintain and operate a domiciliary account designated in foreign currency with an Authorised Dealer.
The foreign currency in which a domiciliary account may be opened, maintained and operated shall be any internationally convertible currency.

Except as provided under any other enactment or law, a person making an application to open a domiciliary account under this Act shall not be obliged to disclose the source of the foreign currency sought to be deposited in the account.
A person may open more than one domiciliary account under this Act designated in the same or different foreign currencies and at the same or in different banks.

An exporter of goods, including petroleum products, shall open and maintain a foreign currency domiciliary account into which may be retained foreign currency corresponding to the entire proceeds of the export concerned.

For external and non-resident non-Nigerian customers, financial institutions shall satisfy themselves that the customer is permanently resident outside Nigeria, and the eligible classes for external accounts are embassies, high commissions, legations or consulates, their career and established members, and other international organisations recognised and accorded diplomatic status and their expatriate officials.

The eligible classes to open non-resident accounts under the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations are overseas correspondence and examination bodies, foreign companies executing approved contracts in Nigeria, and foreign professional bodies.

All accounts of Non-resident stipulated for the external-account and non-resident-account eligible classes shall, on completion of the contract or the applicant’s business in Nigeria, be closed and the balance on the account, if any, transferred to the customer’s account in country of residence, after proper documentation.
candidates.subject: non_resident_account_closure

candidates.candidate_text: Where a customer wishes to open a domiciliary account or make a wholesale deposit by cash or inter-bank transfer, a financial institution shall obtain identification evidence appropriate to individuals, companies, or professional intermediaries, and where funding is by inter-bank transfer the institution shall satisfy itself that the transferring institution is regulated for ML, TF or PF prevention in its country of origin.

Effective 1 January 2025, eligible Non-Resident Nigerians may own a Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account or a Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account subject to meeting KYC requirements, without prejudice to Memorandum 17 of the CBN Foreign Exchange Manual (2018).

A Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account enables Non-Resident Nigerians to remit their foreign earnings to Nigeria and manage funds in both foreign and local currencies; account holders may maintain both a foreign-currency account and/or a Naira account.

A Non-Resident Nigerian Investment Account enables Non-Resident Nigerians to invest in assets in Nigeria in either foreign currency or local currency, and account holders may maintain both a foreign-currency account and/or a Naira account for that purpose.
On 15 May 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria officially launched the Fourth Edition of its Foreign Exchange Manual.

In cases that are not classified under the external-account or non-resident-account eligible classes in the CBN Customer Due Diligence Regulations, financial institutions shall refer to the Central Bank of Nigeria for clarification.
Balances in the foreign-currency account of a Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account can be fully repatriated out of Nigeria without restriction.

Non-Resident Nigerian Ordinary Account holders may maintain a Naira account with funds remitted directly from offshore or convertible from a foreign-currency account at prevailing exchange rates through authorised dealers.
